## R Markdown

## Librarys

```{r}
library(reshape2)
library(e1071)
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot)
library(class)

```

## read Universal Bank file

```{r}
UVBank <- read.csv("C:/Users/ptobo/Desktop/Kent State/3 Fundamentals of Machine Learning BA-64060/Assignments/Assignment 2/UniversalBank.csv")

```

## rename personal loan to loan and credit card to cc, then convert to categorical factor


```{r}

summary(UVBank)


```

```{r}
names(UVBank)[names(UVBank)=="CreditCard"] <- "CC"
names(UVBank)[names(UVBank)=="Personal.Loan"] <- "Loan"
summary(UVBank)
UVBank$CC <- factor(UVBank$CC, levels = c(0,1)) 
UVBank$Loan <- factor(UVBank$Loan, levels = c(0,1))
UVBank$Online <- factor(UVBank$Online, levels = c(0,1))

summary(UVBank)


```

## set seed to 123

```{r}
set.seed(123)

```

## train 60/40

```{r}
train60 <- sample(nrow(UVBank),.6 * nrow(UVBank))
train <- UVBank[train60, ]
valid <- UVBank[-train60, ]

summary(UVBank)
cat("trainedRows:", nrow(train), "validRows", nrow(valid))


```

## melted pivot tables

```{r}
melted <- melt(train, id.vars = c("CC", "Loan", "Online"), measure.vars = "ID")
pivot <-  dcast(melted, CC + Loan ~ Online, fun.aggregate = length)

pivot

```

## group by category, CC w/loan


```{r}
x3 <- pivot[pivot$CC == 1 & pivot$Loan == 1, "1"]
x3

```

## CC, no Loan

```{r}
x2 <- pivot[pivot$CC == 1 & pivot$Loan == 0, "1"]
x2

```

## pivot table probability 

```{r}
prob_x <- x3 / (x3 + x2)
prob_x

```



## naive bayes catagories

```{r}
Loan_Online <-  table(Loan = train$Loan, Online = train$Online)
Loan_CC <- table(Loan = train$Loan, CC = train$CC)

Loan_Online

Loan_CC



```

```{r}
Loan_Online

```

```{r}
Loan_CC

```


## Compute the following quantities means “the probability of A given B”


```{r}
p_i <- Loan_CC["1","1"] / sum(Loan_CC["1",])
p_i

```

```{r}
p_ii <- Loan_Online["1", "1"] / sum(Loan_Online["1", ])
p_ii

```

```{r}
p_iii <- mean(train$Loan == 1)
p_iii

```

```{r}
p_iv <- Loan_CC["0", "1"] / sum(Loan_CC["0", ])
p_iv
```

```{r}
p_v <- Loan_Online["0", "1"] / sum(Loan_Online["0", ])
p_v
```

```{r}
p_vi <- mean(train$Loan == 0)

p_vi


```

## Naive Bayes (NB) probability

```{r}
Numerator <- p_i * p_ii * p_iii
Denominator <-  Numerator + p_iv * p_v * p_vi
P_NB <- Numerator/Denominator
P_NB

```

```{r}
NB <- naiveBayes(Loan ~ CC + Online, data = train)

NB

```

## new customer

```{r}
New_Customer <- data.frame(CC = factor(1, levels = c(0,1)), Online = factor(1, levels = c(0, 1)))
New_Customer

predict(NB, New_Customer, type = "raw")[, "1"]


```

## Based on comparison of the Pivot table results; (prob_x <- x3 / (x3 + x2) = 0.1071429) vs (predict(NB, New_Customer, type = "raw")[, "1"]) = 0.1105637, Pivot probability is more accurate based on zero assumptions with smaller datasets, whereas NB uses small biased assumptions used to identify patterns resulting in a slightly higher prediction value that may be considered negligible.
